Provisional results showed that 70% of voters backed the changes. Under the new constitution, the president will be able to appoint and sack the prime minister and cabinet, create or abolish ministries, and dissolve parliament in a serious political crisis. The reforms also reduced the number of parliamentary seats and electoral constituencies, but retained the five-year presidential term and two-term limit. The military leaders who seized power after a disputed vote in November 2025 say the changes are needed to put an end to repeated political bickering and instability.

The ICG partners are the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) and the World Health Organization (WHO). The initiative builds on the Access and Allocation Mechanism established in 2024 during the last mpox Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC), and will ensure that countries have timely and equitable access to vaccines for outbreak response. Mpox continues to cause outbreaks globally, with two-thirds of reported cases occurring in the African Region.

In a new report released Wednesday, UNEP said crossing 1.5°C would expose countries and communities to escalating climate risks, including more extreme weather, ecosystem losses, threats to food and water security and potentially irreversible changes to major climate systems. The report, Limiting Overshoot , says the most viable remaining pathway is to allow warming to peak and then drive temperatures back down through deep emissions cuts and carefully governed carbon dioxide removal. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The report's central message, however, is that crossing 1.5°C must not become a new climate normal. stories.title: 'The crowd shouted that we'd stolen someone's genitals' - deadly rumours spread on social media
stories.summary: Image source, Alfred Lasteck / BBC Image caption, Boniface Mgala and a friend were pulled out of a restaurant and attacked by a mob that accused them of stealing a man's genitals By Mungai Ngige ,Â BBC Global Disinformation Unit Â and Â Alfred Lasteck ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Tunduma Published 9 hours ago More than 80 people were killed between October 2025 and July this year following false accusations about what is termed "genital theft", the BBC Global Disinformation Unit has found after gathering data from police forces across six African countries. The killings are linked to rumours that a simple tap on the shoulder can cause a man's genitals to shrink or disappear. They are being fuelled by widespread misinformation on social media. "They were shouting that we had stolen someone's genitals and we didn't have any way to escape because there was a huge crowd," Tanzanian mechanic Boniface Mgala told the BBC about his ordeal in April when he was badly beaten by those convinced he was a genital thief. His experience was similar to those in videos seen by the BBC: men claim that their genital organs - penis and testicles - have vanished or shrivelled after coming into contact with strangers and a mob then demands that alleged perpetrators return what they have supposedly stolen. Such claims are rooted in longstanding fears and superstitions - and are not new on the continent, particularly in communities where belief in witchcraft remains widespread.

stories.title: Sharpeville massacre survivors start legal fight for justice in South Africa
stories.summary: Image caption, Abraham Mofokeng was 20 when he joined a peaceful protest in Sharpeville By Pumza Fihlani Reporting from Sharpeville Published 3 September 2026, 01:14 BST Abraham Mofokeng still carries the wounds of the bloody suppression of a protest in South Africa 66 years ago. In what became known as the Sharpeville massacre, police infamously opened fire on thousands of peaceful demonstrators. A bullet is still lodged in Mofokeng's spine, and he has a gentle limp from a gunshot to the leg. "We weren't seen as people," the 86-year-old tells the BBC as he explains the reasons he joined the demonstration on 21 March 1960 against the repressive laws of the white-minority government. "All you were good for was working. You couldn't question them, you were supposed to just do as you're told." The massacre at Sharpeville, which he survived, exposed to the world the violence of the racist apartheid system - yet thanks to an indemnity law passed a year after the killings, none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted. Mofokeng is now part of a legal case set to be announced on Thursday that will seek to overturn this law.

stories.title: Tunisia's activists decry civil society crackdown
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5JrLK Tunisians have been protesting against President Kais Saied this summer, demanding the restoration of democracy and calling for the release of jailed activists and journalists amid a worsening economic and social crisis Image: Jihed Abidellaoui/REUTERS Advertisement "Most civil society organizations are in a state of shock today," Messaoud Romdhani, a Tunisian human rights activist told DW. "Those who criticize the authorities or situation in Tunisia face widespread repression," he explained, adding that "most have been accused of money laundering, which leads to the suspension of their activities." Another Tunisian activist, who spoke with DW on condition of anonymity, also said that increasingly people were thinking twice before speaking in public or even choosing to work on sensitive issues. "What worries me most is the chilling effect: When organizations face suspension and activists face prosecution or detention , the uncertainty itself becomes a form of pressure," he said. Human Rights Watch has also raised the alarm. In its latest report , published Wednesday morning, the international rights watchdog concludes that Saied is attempting to shutter Tunisia's civil society entirely. "It is clear that the authorities are abusing every tool at their disposal to close the space for civil society in Tunisia," the report reads. The watchdog also points out that civil society groups in Tunisia have played a key role in holding power to account, delivering essential services and advocating for people's human rights . "The government has used abusive, arbitrary prosecutions, detentions, financial investigations and suspension of organizations in an attempt to stifle these voices," Bassam Khawaja, a deputy director in the Middle East and North Africa Division at Human Rights Watch and editor of the report, told DW. He added that it was clear the idea was to shut down all opposition and independent voices in the country. "This amounts to a total crackdown on civil society in Tunisia," he said.

Photograph: Sipa US/Alamy Sweden ends aid to Liberia in a hammer blow to women’s rights and healthcare Sexual and reproductive services face an uncertain future as the country’s second-largest donor halts support worth hundreds of millions of pounds T he Swedish flag is still flying above the pale blue building overlooking the Atlantic in Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, but the doors of the embassy are now closed to visitors. On 31 August, the Swedish embassy in Liberia ends a presence in the country that dates back to 1961. The billions of kronor of aid that Sweden pipes into the west African country will end on the same day, as sweeping cuts to Swedish development funding come into effect.

stories.title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
stories.summary: As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July and the start of August. Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the end of July and the start of August. Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migration Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said there is no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta but accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation. As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration .

stories.title: ‘We want to find a better future’: teenage girls on why they risked their lives to reach Spain
stories.summary: Composite: Soraya Aybar Laafou View image in fullscreen Composite: Soraya Aybar Laafou ‘We want to find a better future’: teenage girls on why they risked their lives to reach Spain More than two dozen teenagers stuck in the Spanish territory of Ceuta shared their reasons for joining the treacherous mass crossing in July For Fatin, one of the teenage girls now living in limbo in a makeshift camp in the Spanish city of Ceuta, the decision to leave her home in Morocco began to form when she had to give up school. She wanted to continue studying, she says, but at home she was expected to take responsibility for the housework instead. As classes and learning gave way to domestic chores, the future she had imagined for herself began to feel increasingly distant. Fatin was one of 29 girls who shared their feelings about their past and future with the Guardian. All of them had been part of the mass crossing from Morocco in late July that made headlines around the world.

stories.title: Nurture not nature? How young women can learn to better wield economic power | Heather Stewart
stories.summary: Groups of 12- and 13-year-old girls were given just 12 hours of negotiation classes, over three weeks. Photograph: MBI/Alamy View image in fullscreen Groups of 12- and 13-year-old girls were given just 12 hours of negotiation classes, over three weeks. Photograph: MBI/Alamy How young women can learn to better wield economic power Heather Stewart Project in Zambia shows how teaching young women to negotiate better can have a long-term impact on their prospects W omen making their way in patriarchal societies down the ages have always had to wield their meagre economic power deftly. New evidence from a fascinating research project in Zambia suggests that’s a skill that can be learned. A team of female US academics have been gathering data for more than a decade, which shows that teaching young women to negotiate better can have a long-term impact on their prospects.

stories.title: People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city
stories.summary: Save the Children, citing government figures, says more than 200,000 people fled to El Obeid in the first half of the year. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Save the Children, citing government figures, says more than 200,000 people fled to El Obeid in the first half of the year. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city More traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirts Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside. The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children. “The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety. The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.” The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.

stories.title: Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid
stories.summary: The 200-carat platinum and diamond-encrusted necklace. Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/Getty View image in fullscreen The 200-carat platinum and diamond-encrusted necklace. Photograph: Stéphane de Sakutin/AFP/Getty Egyptian queen’s 673-diamond necklace stolen in Vienna smash-and-grab raid Police hunt two suspects after historic 200-carat piece is snatched from Austrian museum during opening hours Austrian police are hunting two men alleged to have stolen a 200-carat platinum necklace encrusted with 673 diamonds that was on loan to a museum in Vienna and once belonged to Egyptian royalty. Authorities in the capital released pictures of the suspects captured by security cameras during the heist at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK), amid a rash of spectacular smash-and-grab thefts from European cultural institutions. The unmasked men bought tickets to the exhibition before shattering a glass display case with a hammer during opening hours on Thursday afternoon and making off with the diamond necklace.

stories.title: World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, King Oyo ascended to the throne at the age of three but was crowned on reaching adulthood at 18 in 2010 By Swaibu Ibrahim BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Kampala Published 28 August 2026 A traditional Ugandan ruler named as the world's youngest monarch has died aged 34, his prime minister has announced. Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV became king of Tooro in western Uganda at just three years old in 1995 after the death of his father. The Tooro kingdom did not disclose the cause of King Oyo's death, but a Ugandan government minister was quoted in local media saying that he had been critically ill and was seeking treatment in the US. Though Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, it has several traditional kingdoms which continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power. Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch , external , ruled over more than two million people.

stories.title: ‘Behind every case, a person’: the man leading DRC’s Ebola fight on the human cost hidden behind the numbers
stories.summary: Congolese medical workers in PPE carry children tested and cleared of Ebola in Bunia town, Ituri province, DRC. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters View image in fullscreen Congolese medical workers in PPE carry children tested and cleared of Ebola in Bunia town, Ituri province, DRC. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters Interview ‘Behind every case, a person’: the man leading DRC’s Ebola fight on the human cost hidden behind the numbers Tracy McVeigh Prof Pierre Akilimali, who heads DR Congo’s response to an outbreak that has so far killed more than 2,700 people, says tackling the disease requires trust and respect T he statistics, says the man responsible for overseeing the Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), are meaningless. That it is now the largest outbreak, the most deadly strain, that 100 days have passed, that the death rates keep climbing, says Prof Pierre Akilimali, should never detract from the human tragedies at the centre of this virus. “It is behind those numbers that matters; it is the father, the child, the loved relative. Behind every case is a person and behind every person is a family.

stories.title: Africa: Africa CDC Unveils Statue Honoring Dr. Senait Fisseha
stories.summary: Africa CDC Unveils Statue Honoring Dr. Senait Fisseha (left), Vice President of Global Programs at the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation, is congratulated by Dr. Jean Kaseya, Director-General of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, after the unveiling of a statue at Africa CDC headquarters in Addis Ababa, "recognising her leadership, partnership and longstanding commitment to strengthening African institutions and advancing health across the continent." 26 August 2026 Content from a Premium Partner Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — A special moment at Africa CDC today as we welcomed Dr. Senait Fisseha, Vice President of Global Programs at the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation. During her visit, Africa CDC unveiled a surprise statue in her honour, recognising her leadership, partnership and longstanding commitment to strengthening African institutions and advancing health across the continent.
